subject: Cooking
title: Potatoes: How a Root Saved Europe
description: A micro-lesson that makes Potatoes: How a Root Saved Europe usable.

hook.text: Europeans refused to eat potatoes for over a century. Then they prevented a continent from starving.

buildup.text: Spanish conquistadors brought potatoes from Peru in the 1530s, but Europeans viewed them with suspicion.

discovery.text: Potatoes yield 2-4 times more calories per acre than grain — a lifesaver for growing populations.

twist.text: Frederick the Great of Prussia forced peasants to plant potatoes. He posted guards around royal potato fields.

climax.text: By 1800, the potato fed most of Northern Europe. Its failure in Ireland caused a devastating famine.

punchline.text: A Peruvian root became Europe's most important food.

quiz.question: Where did potatoes originate before arriving in Europe?

details.summary: The potato, imported from South America in the 1500s, took 200 years to gain acceptance in Europe before becoming the continent's most important food crop. It could feed more people per acre than any grain, ending cycles of famine across northern Europe.
details.whyItMatters: The potato transformed European history by solving centuries of famine, enabling population growth, and providing the caloric foundation for industrialization. Its story shows how a single crop can reshape civilization.
takeaways: Potatoes yield 2 to 4 times more calories per acre than grain crops
Europeans initially rejected potatoes as poisonous or unChristian
The Irish Potato Famine killed one million and displaced another million

faq.question: Why did Europeans resist eating potatoes for so long?
faq.answer: As a nightshade family member, potatoes were associated with toxic plants. They grew underground, which superstitious Europeans considered unnatural. The Bible did not mention potatoes, making some clergy suspicious.

faq.question: How did the potato change European population growth?
faq.answer: Between 1700 and 1900, European population tripled, and historians attribute a significant portion to potato adoption. Potatoes provided more calories per acre than wheat, survived in poor soil and cold climates, and required less labor.
